sources.news_title: OpenAI said most activity involved routine research, while some agents used exposed credentials or tried to breach sites, and 53 user images were posted online.

OpenAI’s autonomous agents probed U.S. government websites this summer without the company noticing.
The agents interacted with sites operated by the Education Department, the Commerce Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), according to the New York Times. OpenAI has confirmed the Commerce and SEC episodes while it keeps investigating what happened at Education.
At the Education Department, the software tried and failed to break into the civil rights office in search of data, according to researchers at the AI firm Transluce. At Commerce, the agents pulled Census Bureau figures after finding login credentials in public code repositories, Politico reported. They also copied public material from SEC.gov and Investor.gov and reposted it on a separate site. (RELATED: First Hugging Face, Now Australia: OpenAI Agents Hack Their Way Into A Government)
None of the activity counted as a breach, OpenAI said. The company found no misused SEC credentials, no account access, no nonpublic data and no changes to SEC data or systems, according to the Associated Press (AP). Chief Executive Sam Altman called it an “extensive and ongoing review related to our agents’ use of internet access during training and evaluation” in a social media post, AP reported.
Breaking News: OpenAI’s technology went rogue and meddled with three U.S. government websites this summer without the A.I. lab’s knowledge. https://t.co/6kfc7qzrsh
— The New York Times (@nytimes) September 25, 2026
SEC spokesperson Kurt Hopfenspirger said “no non-public information was accessed,” according to Politico. An Education Department spokesperson said reviews found “no evidence of any impact to our website or databases,” the Times reported. A Commerce official said the Census data was already public and held nothing private.
Transluce also found rogue behavior it could not firmly tie to OpenAI, reaching the Justice Department and state sites in California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas and New York, the AP reported. Probing of Navy and White House budget office sites could not be traced to any single lab, according to the Times.
The episodes follow an OpenAI agent’s break-in at an Australian health data portal in June, called the first known case of an AI system hacking a government network, according to Nature. OpenAI traced a July attack on the startup Hugging Face to two of its most capable models, according to the AP.
Republican California Rep. Jay Obernolte called it “another example of a loss of human control” on CNN. Democratic California Rep. Ted Lieu gave a similar warning about the technology, saying, “It will relentlessly try to complete a task, and it doesn’t understand morality and consequences and evil and good,” according to the Times.

OpenAI acknowledged Friday that its AI agents interacted with several U.S. government websites in unexpected ways, as the company's review of unauthorized model activity continues to grow in scope.
The SEC, the Census Bureau, and the Department of Education were among the sites reached, as independent researchers identified additional incidents
The company said its models accessed publicly available information on two Securities and Exchange Commission websites — SEC.gov and Investor.gov — as well as demographic and economic data from the Census Bureau using publicly available developer keys. OpenAI said it found no evidence of a compromise, credential misuse, or access to nonpublic information at either agency. Agents also attempted, without success, to access the Department of Education, whose spokesperson told CNBC that system reviews found "no evidence of any impact to our website or databases."
Independent AI research lab Transluce separately reported that agents it believes may be linked to OpenAI made failed attempts in May to retrieve an image from a University of New Mexico digital library and, while seeking data about the University of Iowa, to pull records from a public platform called Data USA, according to CNBC. Transluce also found what it described as a rudimentary, unsuccessful attempt to access a Department of Education civil rights website, according to NPR. The lab said it also found additional activity, not all of it attributable to OpenAI, targeting the Justice Department, the Commerce Department, and state government sites in California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas, and New York. OpenAI said it is reviewing the Transluce report.
"Most of the activity we've reviewed so far involved routine research tasks, such as accessing public web content to answer questions," an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC. "Some involved government websites because our models often turn to them as authoritative sources of public information."
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote on X $TWTR that the company has launched an "extensive and ongoing review" examining how its agents used internet access during training and evaluation, and has been publishing summaries of what it finds. He said the review is complicated by the scale of agent activity logs involved and the need to work with affected organizations. The Hugging Face breach, Altman said, "is still the most severe event we've seen."
"There is an extensive and ongoing review related to our agents’ use of internet access during training and evaluation. We’ve been publishing summaries at the link below and will continue to," Altman said. "We have not been as fast as we would have liked but we are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding from petabytes of agent activity logs, and working with impacted organizations."
OpenAI's misalignment review began after the company disclosed in July that autonomous agents escaped a controlled testing environment and breached Hugging Face, an open-source AI developer platform. The incident prompted OpenAI to halt portions of its model development and introduce new security measures. This week, the company published eight additional reports on its misalignment disclosure page detailing unexpected model behaviors observed during training, including agents that used internal systems as message boards and models that added unauthorized instructions to their own summaries.
On Thursday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorized access to Australia's Medicare statistics database in June, pulling both public and non-public files. He described OpenAI's notification to the Australian government — an email sent to a generic government address in September — as "unacceptable." OpenAI said it became aware of the breach in August.
OpenAI said most cases identified so far have been low severity, but that completing the full review will take months.
